newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan delight at yen rise sets scene for more.
newsitem.headline: Japan delight at yen rise sets scene for more.

text.p: Comments by Japanese Finance Ministry officials at the weekend that they were delighted with the yen's dramatic rise against the dollar has set the scene for a lively week in foreign exchange markets.

With the official boost to guide them, most traders expect the Japanese currency to add to the nearly four yen rise it recorded against the dollar last Friday, capping a rally of nearly six yen for the the week.

Looking ahead to next week, traders have zeroed in on remarks Saturday by the country's "Mr Yen", senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, who said last week's gains were "not overly excessive."
Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau, was so delighted that he even joked about how markets had finally got the message about a stronger yen.
"It's like cold Japanese sake. It takes time to hit you. Which means it does not hit you immediately," he said.
The talk-up-the-yen weekend ended on Sunday with a statement by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at a news conference that the yen's surge against the dollar was a favourable development.

"My understanding of the currency markets in the past several days, which show a correction in the yen's weakness, is that the G7's strong resolve has started to penetrate the markets," Mitsuzuka said.

Financial leaders of the G7 -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- had said in Washington last month that they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate. They said currency values should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was not desirable.
Both Sakakibara and Mitsuzuka were talking in the southern Japanese city of Fukuoka where they were attending the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank (ADB).
However both men plan to be back at their desks in Tokyo for the opening of markets on Monday.
Mitsuzuka clearly warned that if markets started to move in the wrong direction again there would be intervention.
"As for the future, we will continue to monitor the markets closely and with take appropriate steps at the appropriate times," he said.
Until last week, the dollar was supported by expectations of higher U.S. rates and continued low rates in Japan.

But a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Friday appearing to back away from a rise in short-term U.S. interest rates, and speculation of higher rates in Japan led traders to re-evaluate expectations and send the dollar lower.
On Friday, the drop accelerated, tumbling below the key 120 yen threshold in New York to its lowest point since January 27.
Bank of Tokyo economist Soichi Enkyo said the comments by Sakakibara and others would not move markets greatly but will support current trends.

"Sakakibara's comments will only serve to remind the markets of what the G7 has already agreed on the question of the yen-dollar rate. So talking about it now will only support what they have already said.
There have already been changes in the yen's value and this may continue what with America's economy under a certain strain and Japan upping long-term interest rates," Enkyo said.
